extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of 18th-century English literature; literary scholars
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting evaluative principles and production standards for early-18th-century periodical essays, comedies, opera libretti, and theatrical adaptation as exemplified by Addison, Steele, and contemporaries. Emphasises what makes dramatic and periodical writing effective or objectionable in that period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive didacticism
rubrics_metrics.description: The book was 'too didactic' and an 'air of superiority' belongs to a too didactic manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Didactic tone, where the author speaks with an assumed superiority or teaches rules overtly, is repugnant to Steele's nature and weakens literary effect. Writers should avoid a manner that reads like a professional teaching rules of their own art; truth is better conveyed without overbearing moral instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Base comedy upon seriousness (earnest thought underpinning wit)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each comedy of Steele's was based on seriousness; 'The gay manner did not conceal all the earnest thoughts.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comedic works should be grounded in serious ideas or moral purpose rather than mere frivolity. Wit and gaiety are effective when they serve and do not obscure earnest criticism or ethical aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid coarse language and unwholesome expletives in stage comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Steele's comedies 'were wholly free from the garnish of oaths and unwholesome expletives which his contemporaries seemed to think essential to stage emphasis.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refrain from relying on profanity or crude expletives for emphasis; cleaner language can coexist with wit and still achieve stage effect and moral acceptability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not sacrifice art to piety—maintain genre integrity
rubrics_metrics.description: Changes in Steele's adaptation of the 'Menteur' made it 'beyond the bounds of comedy' — 'excellent morality but not good art.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral or pious intent must not override the structural and aesthetic demands of the genre. Avoid transforming a comedy into a moral tract; preserve the genre's conventions so art remains effective while conveying moral themes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure theatrical effects are strong enough for the audience (strokes must 'appear at a distance')
rubrics_metrics.description: A stage-piece must not be 'like a picture in which the strokes were not strong enough to appear at a distance'—subtleties can be lost on a popular assembly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing for performance, make characterisation, plot beats, and comic/business sufficiently pronounced for a live audience; delicate touches may be appreciated by readers or critics but fail in popular theatre unless staged with care.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blend pleasure with severity ('Pleasure must still have something that's severe')
rubrics_metrics.description: Steele (adapting a line) wrote in his Prologue: 'Pleasure must still have something that's severe.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Entertainments should include an element of seriousness or moral gravity; reforming or morally-minded audiences expect gaiety to be tempered by severity or instructive content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use drama to criticise social vices without mere ridicule
rubrics_metrics.description: Steele attacked duelling and the 'mockery and mummery of grief' in his plays; he blended censure with lively comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dramatic works can and should censure social vices (e.g., duelling, mock grief, legal mockery) by integrating earnest critique into characters and plot, rather than resorting solely to ridicule or sentimentality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opera libretti should be written in excellent English and support English music
rubrics_metrics.description: Thomas Clayton argued that 'the words of an opera should be not only English, but the best of English, and that English music ought to illustrate good home-grown literature.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing opera in English, libretti should employ high-quality English diction and verse; the musical setting should serve and illustrate the literary qualities of the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Periodical papers should balance serious matters with light diversion
rubrics_metrics.description: Defoe's Review: 'After our Serious Matters are over, we shall at the end of every Paper, Present you with a little Diversion...'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successful periodicals mix earnest political or moral discussion with lighter entertainments or diversions; this pacing keeps readers engaged while addressing substantial topics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satirical censure should target actions and vices, not persons or party labels
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'Scandalous Club' resolves 'to censure the Actions of Men, not of Parties... They do not design to expose Persons but things... they resolve to treat Vice, and Villanous Actions, with the utmost Severity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satire and public censure are most defensible and effective when aimed at publicly observable actions or vices rather than personal attacks or partisan persecution; focus criticism on conduct, not identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delicate touches and 'Molière-like' subtleties reward careful readers and actors
rubrics_metrics.description: Addison's play was noted as having scenes 'drawn after Molière's manner' with 'an easy and natural vein of humour' and 'touches being too delicate for every taste in a popular assembly.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers may incorporate refined, subtle humour and characterisation in the Molière tradition, but should be aware that such subtleties require discerning performers and audiences to be fully appreciated; consider medium and audience when choosing subtlety levels.
